analytic.title: Dynamic Voltage Scaling for Power-aware Hierarchical Real-Time Scheduling Framework

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Recent research on hierarchical real-time scheduling framework has made it feasible to build large and complex real-time systems. A hierarchical real-time scheduling framework decomposes a system into multiple components which are composed of other sub-components. The component schedulability is analyzed based on the periodic resource model, where each component is guaranteed with a certain amount of periodic resource supply per resource period. Although most of researches have focused on efficient scheduling of a component's task set, little work has been done on power-aware scheduling in hierarchical real-time scheduling framework, which has become an important issue in many recent real-time embedded applications. In this paper, we define a new problem for power-aware scheduling in hierarchical framework with periodic resource model. We provide optimal task-level and component-level static DVS (Dynamic Voltage Scaling) schemes. A component-level dynamic DVS scheme is also provided in order to reduce more energy at run-time.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Computer software technology has been enormously grown in functionality and complexity, which makes it difficult to be thoroughly designed and maintained. In order to design and build large and complex real-time systems, componentbased system design has been widely accepted as methodology for composing the system through systematic abstraction and composition. Component-based design assures that designers can decompose a system into multiple components and focus on designing individual component. In addition, componentbased system design enables components to be reused in other environments.

In a hierarchical or compositional real-time scheduling framework, the main problem is to define a scheduling interface model in order to specify the collective real-time requirements of a component. Many frameworks [1], [3], [2], [4], [5], [6] have been proposed for different real-time models. In [1], a hierarchical real-time virtual resource model that permits resource partitioning to be extended to multiple levels is introduced. Through this model, partitions on each level are scheduled as if they had access to a dedicated resource and there is minimal interference between neighboring partition levels.

In [4], a periodic resource model is proposed for compositional real-time scheduling frameworks supporting periodic task model. The periodic resource model describes the behavior of a periodic resource and calculates its minimum resource allocations in a time interval. A periodic resource Γ(Π, Θ) guarantees to supply at each resource period Π exactly Θ computational time units to a component. Shin and Lee [2] extended this framework to support the bounded-delay task model and developed an exact schedulability condition. Shin et al. [3] presented a hierarchical scheduling framework for virtual clustering of multiprocessors. In their framework, processors are organized into a hierarchy of virtual clusters; each containing a set of physical multiprocessors. To support the imprecise computation task model, Tchamgoue et al. [5] proposed the imprecise resource model Γ(Π, Θ, Ω) to guarantee at every resource period Π, at least Θ and at most Θ + Ω computation time units.

As power-consumption becomes an important issue in recent real-time embedded systems, lots of work has been suggested to reduce energy with the real-time constraints. One of common techniques for reducing dynamic power consumption is based on Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS) scheme which scales the processor frequency dynamically. Since there are tradeoffs between execution time and power consumption, many studies have been done on RT-DVS (Real-Time Dynamic Voltage Scaling) problem [7] for aperiodic [9], [10] and periodic tasks [11], [12], [7]. RT-DVS schemes utilizes slack times to adjust the processor speed without violating tasks deadlines.

As multiprocessor and multi-core technologies have been developing rapidly, RT-DVS problem in multiprocessors has been dealt with in many recent studies. Guan et al. presented test conditions for non-preemptive EDF (Earliest Deadline First) and fixed priority scheduling [17]. Aydin et al. considered the energy-aware partitioning of real-time tasks for multiprocessor systems [18]. Chen et al. proposed a real-time scheduling method that minimizes both dynamic and leakage energy consumption in multiprocessor systems [8]. The energy reduction becomes a hot issue even in Cloud computing which requires huge amount of computing power [19].

In our earlier work [6], we provided a new model for poweraware hierarchical real-time scheduling framework. However, the work lacks specific scheduling algorithms. Thus, we focus on DVS scheduling algorithms for the purpose of reducing the energy consumption of a component. The main contributions of this paper include: (i) defining a new problem of poweraware scheduling in a periodic resource model; (ii) providing optimal solutions for static task-level and component-level DVS scheme; and (iii) suggesting an online DVS scheme for power-aware scheduling in hierarchical real-time framework.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II defines the system model including hierarchical real-time scheduling framework and power model, and categorizes DVS schemes in the framework. In Section III, we provide the schedulability analysis of static DVS schemes. Section IV provides optimal static DVS schemes in a component, while Section V describes an online DVS scheme. We evaluate the proposed schemes using simulations in Section VI, and concludes the paper with a summary and the future work.

div.head: II. POWER-AWARE SCHEDULING IN HIERARCHICAL REAL-TIME SCHEDULING FRAMEWORK
A. Hierarchical real-time scheduling framework
div.p: In a hierarchical scheduling framework, a component is the basic scheduling unit and is defined by C(W, R, A), where W is the task set in the component, R is the resource model from the upper component, and A is the scheduling algorithm [2], [4]. Components are organized hierarchically so that a upper-layer component allocates resource to its lowerlayer components, as shown in Figure 1.

A component task set W consists of n periodic real-time tasks. Each task τ i is defined by (p i , e i ), so that task τ i releases a job every p i time units. The j-th job of task τ i denoted by J i,j should be finished by the next job's release time.

A resource model in hierarchical real-time scheduling framework specifies the amount of resource to be allocated to a component. In this paper, we use the periodic resource model proposed in [2], [4]. A periodic resource model Γ(Π, Θ) guarantees that the resource amount of Θ time units is supplied every Π time units to a component. For example, the resource model Γ 1 (10, 3) of component C 1 in Figure 1 guarantees the resource of 3 time units is provided to the component every 10 time units.

div.head: B. Power model
div.p: Let us consider an application with the execution time t running on a processor with its maximum frequency f max . If the processor runs at the frequency level f (0 < f ≤ f max ), the relative processor level is given by f /f max . Thus, the application execution time on the processor with the speed level S (0 < S ≤ 1) is defined by t/S, where t is the execution time on the maximum processor speed level. That is, the application execution time is slowed down by the factor of S.

The energy consumption of a processor core is composed of dynamic and static energy. In this work, we only consider the dynamic energy consumption, as it is a dominating factor in the total energy consumption [14] and is managed by the DVS (Dynamic Voltage Scaling) scheme. The dynamic energy is generally in proportion to the cubic of the frequency f . Let us assume that an application execution time is given by t under the maximum processor speed. Then, the energy consumption of the application on the processor speed level S is defined by
div.formula: E = α • t S • S 3 = α • t • S 2 ,
div.p: where α is a coefficient. In this paper, we assume α = 1 for the sake of simplicity.

div.head: C. Power-aware scheduling in periodic resource model
div.p: As shown in Figure 1, the local scheduler of a component has a Dynamic Power Management (DPM) unit of which role is to scale the processor speed level. The component scheduler is assumed to be able to adjust the processor speed level dynamically if necessary. Thus, the power-aware real-time scheduling problem in periodic resource model is to minimize the energy consumption of real-time tasks without violating tasks deadlines where a resource of Θ time units is provided every Π time units.

In this paper, the DVS scheme can be static or dynamic. The static DVS scheme assigns a processor speed level to each task or component before the system runs. In the other hand, the dynamic scheme varies the speed level dynamically at run-time. In addition, the DVS scheme is applied to task level, component level, or system level in hierarchical realtime scheduling framework. So, we will discuss the following power-aware scheduling problems in this paper.

1) Task-level static DVS scheduling (in Section IV.A): For each task in a component, the relative speed level of the processor is determined. So, the local scheduler adjusts the processor speed level to the pre-defined value of the task whenever it is executed. 2) Component-level static DVS scheduling (in Section IV.B): While a component is running, the processor is set to a given speed level S C . The optimal speed level S C not only guarantees the schedulability of the component's tasks, but also minimizes the energy consumption of the component.

div.head: 3) System-level static DVS scheduling (in Section IV.C):
div.p: The processor runs at a given speed level S P during its run-time. Tasks in all components in the hierarchy are executed on the specified processor speed level. An optimal speed level S P minimizes the total energy consumption and guarantees the schedulability of all tasks as well. 4) Component-level dynamic DVS scheduling (in Section V): A component scheduler decides the processor speed level every resource period at the time when a periodic resource is released. The scheduler adjusts its relative speed for the purpose of minimizing the total energy consumption while meeting all the deadlines.

div.head: III. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS OF POWER-AWARE SCHEDULING
div.p: It is very difficult to reason about power optimization in a hierarchical scheduling framework at system level. Therefore, in this section, we will focus our discussion only on component and task levels power-aware scheduling problems.

div.head: A. Component-level DVS scheduling
div.p: First, we focus on power-aware real-time scheduling in a component level. A component is provided with a periodic resource Γ(Π, Θ) which guarantees to supply a computational time interval of Θ units every Π period. The demand and supply bound analysis in [4] is used to analyze the feasibility of tasks in a component for a given resource model. If the demand bound of tasks is less than or equal to the supply bound of the resource model, tasks are guaranteed to be scheduled in their deadlines.

Let us assume that the processor slows down its speed level to s during the execution of a component C. Since the feasibility analysis in [4] assumes the maximum speed level of a processor, a new feasibility analysis is required with consideration of the speed level. This is done by deriving a new demand bound function for a given speed level.
For a periodic resource model Γ(Π, Θ), the resource supply bound function which defines the minimum resource supply for any time interval t is defined by: sbf

Now, we define the power-aware demand bound functions of tasks for a given periodic resource model under the assumption of the processor speed level s. As the processor speed decreases, the resource demand of a task increases. Since e i execution time is defined at the maximum processor speed level, the execution time is increased by e i /s every period.

We define the power-aware demand bound function pdbf W (A, t, s) as the worst-case resource demand of a task set W under the processor speed level s. div.head: IV. OPTIMAL STATIC DVS SCHEMES
div.p: In this Section, we present our solutions for optimal poweraware scheduling at system, component and task levels assuming only the EDF scheduling policy.
A. An optimal task-level static DVS scheme

We first define a new problem for power-aware scheduling of tasks in a hierarchical real-time scheduling framework under a task-level static DVS scheme. Let us denote s i as the processor speed level during the execution of task τ i . In the task-level static scheme, the processor speed is adjusted to s i while task τ i is executing.

For a component task set W of n tasks with a resource model Γ under EDF scheduling algorithm, we want to minimize the total energy consumption τi∈W P pi • ei si • s 3 i where P is the LCM of all p i 's, as long as the schedulability of W is guaranteed. Thus, an optimal task-level static DVS scheduling problem OPT-TSDS is defined by finding s i to minimize This result complies with the work done by Aydin et al. [13] and extends it to hierarchical real-time scheduling frameworks. Thus, exploiting the same solution approach [13], an instance of the OPT-TSDS problem can be solved using the method of Lagrange multipliers in O(mn log n), where m represents the total number of constraints and n is the number of tasks in the workload. The algorithm first finds an optimal solution to the problem by turning the inequalities into equality constraints (this new problem is denoted by OPT). A solution to problem OPT can be derived in many case in time O(m). The solution then proceeds by considering only the equalities and lower bound constraints. The solution to OPT is invoked for each task in order to check the equality constraints and to set the times assigned to each task that violates the constraints to zero. Since a binary-search like technique is used, the time complexity for these operations is O(m log n).

div.head: C. A system-level static DVS scheme
div.p: The system-level optimization is not a trivial problem, so we just describe a simple static DVS scheme based on the component-level optimal solutions as presented below. Suppose that a system consists of N components of which optimal component-level speeds are known as S i for each. Then, the system-level static DVS scheme is to select the maximum S i among all N components in order to guarantee the schedulability of all components.

div.head: V. THE PROPOSED COMPONENT-LEVEL DYNAMIC DVS SCHEME
A. The proposed dynamic DVS scheduling
div.p: In this section, we provide an online component-level DVS scheme under EDF. The resource model Γ guarantees a minimum resource supply every period, but its release time is not known in advance. The static scheme in Section IV is based on the worst-case resource supply so that we need a dynamic DVS scheme in order to save more energy depending on the actual resource arrival time to the component.

As we use EDF for scheduling the jobs, the scheduler manages a waiting queue for released jobs of periodic tasks. The j-th instance or job of a periodic task τ i is denoted as J i,j . Since a periodic job should be finished by the next job's release time, the absolute deadline of job J i,j is defined by j • p i , which is denoted as d a i,j . The EDF scheduling algorithm gives higher priorities to jobs with smaller d a i,j 's. We denote c i,j as the remaining execution time of J i,j under the maximum processor speed. If job J i,j is executed on the processor with speed level s during t time units, the remaining execution time is decreased by t • s.

The proposed DVS scheme decides the processor speed level at the time of periodic resource supply. In this paper, we assume that a periodic resource supply is non-preemptive to other components. That is, when a periodic resource is released at time rt, the resource is available to the component task set by rt + Θ without any preemption. The local scheduler is responsible for scheduling available component's jobs during this resource supply period.

Each job requires different resource utilization as they have different execution times and deadlines. In a single processor with full utilization, the utilization of a job is defined by the remaining execution time divided by the remaining time to its deadline. However, in hierarchical real-time scheduling framework, a component does not use the processor fully so that we need to calculate the remaining resource time available to each job until its deadline.

Let us assume that a periodic resource is released at time rt. The resource time available to job J i,j in the current resource period, denoted as r curr i,j , depends on three cases, as shown in Figure 5.

i) d a i,j ≥ rt + Θ: Since the deadline is greater than rt + Θ, Θ time is available to the job. ii) d a i,j < rt + Θ: As the deadline is between rt and rt + Θ, only rt + Θd a i,j time units are available to the job. iii) rt ≥ (j -1) • p i < rt + Θ: When a new job is released between rt and rt + Θ, the job can be executed only for rt + Θ -(j -1) • p i . Next, we derive the guaranteed resource supply time to a job from the next resource period to the job's deadline. When a job J i,j is released at (j -1)p i time, the number of resource periods just before the resource period including the deadline d a i,j is shown in Figure 6. In the last resource period, the guaranteed resource time for the job can be calculated considering the worst-case, as shown in Figure 6. We denote this guaranteed resource time for job J i,j for the remaining resource periods as r next i,j . The algorithm JobRelease in Figure 7 includes calculating r next i,j at the job release time (lines 20-22). The value of r next i,j is decreased by Θ every resource period (lines 1-2).
When a periodic resource is released, we derive the effective utilization of related jobs as in Eqn. (5).

The JobRelease algorithm describes periodic job releases and includes the calculation of the remaining guaranteed resource amount for a new job. The REU-DVS (Remaining Effective Utilization-based DVS) algorithm is called at the time of resource release (rt) and decides the current component speed level by adding all effective utlizations of the jobs.

So, the proposed online DVS scheme consumes less power compared to the two optimal static DVS schemes. set the resource period to Π = 5 time units throughout the evaluation and varied the resource supply Θ by 0.5 from 1.5 to 5 time units. We implemented a prototype of the dynamic algorithm and statically computed the optimal speed values for component-level and task-level algorithms. The simulation was done on the hyperperiod (i.e. 600 time units) including the resource period. The total energy for each algorithm is plotted in Figure 9. We normalized the total energy with respect to that of the maximum speed level. As shown in Figure 9, the proposed algorithms reduce much energy compared to the native EDF that runs tasks at maximum processor speed without DVS.

The results of Figure 9 clearly show that the energy curves decrease as more resource is provided to component. The optimal task-level static scheme performs better than the optimal component-level algorithm. However, the dynamic algorithm provides more energy reduction than both static schemes. This is due to the fact that static schemes consider only the worstcase execution time of tasks and not the dynamic character of the resource availability. For this simulation, we let the resource to be released at random times at every resource supply.

The static component and the static task level schemes reduce the energy respectively by about 84% and 88% while the dynamic component policy can save the energy up to 95% in average. However, as the resource supply increases, the three algorithms tend to converge and provide close amount of energy. As suggested in [7], a good utilization scenario may be to combine one of the static schemes with the dynamic policy. Thus, optimal speed values will be computed statically and used at runtime as initial speed values. The online policy will then concentrate on using the unused resource slots to provide more energy saving.

In order to know what scheme to favor for a given resource supply, we compared the algorithms over different resource supplies. We considered the following nine resource supplies: {Γ(2, 1), Γ(3, 1.5), Γ(4, 2), Γ(5, 2.5), Γ(6, 3), Γ(7, 3. As resource period becomes fine, the resource can be utilized more efficiently not only for schedulability, but also for energy reduction. This result can be useful for the system designer to decide the optimal resource supply for each component considering the energy consumption of the whole system. However, it is worthy to note that a finer resource period increases the number of context switches and thenceforth the overall system overhead. Therefore, there is a tradeoff between the number of context switches and the period of the resource.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we defined a new problem of power-aware scheduling in the periodic resource model for hierarchical realtime scheduling framework. The DVS scheme can be applied in task-level, component-level, or system-level in hierarchical framework. We solved an optimal static DVS scheme based on EDF in both task-level and component-level. We also provided a component-level online DVS scheme which decides the processor speed level of a component dynamically. As it utilizes periodic resource arrival information as well as the guaranteed amount of resource, the dynamic DVS scheme reduces more energy than static schemes, as shown throughout simulations.

We are currently focusing on more analysis of poweraware scheduling including the proposed schemes. For example, we can imporve the proposed dynamic DVS scheme by extending it into task-level DVS schemes. In addition, we plan to investigate more optimization (e.g. system-level energy minimization), and implement the proposed scheme in RTLinux-based systems.
